5284.prule: In the 18th-century Tarahumara recorded by Steffel (mostly Tomochic district, 1763-65), word stress is lexically contrastive and not predictable (minimal pairs guacá/guáca, hulí/húli), but confined to an initial three-syllable window: 97% of 1086 reliably accented words carry one stress on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable (9% / 60% / 28%); disyllables are 94% final(=2nd)-stressed, trisyllables split 42% second vs 47% third, 4-syllable words 72% second. qtr.text: Nothing, or almost nothing, can be said about accent - much less about tone - in Quepo, since, first, no word of this language has survived; second, the materials available for this study do not allow accentual positions to be identified, owing to the scarcity of data. In some cases vowel alternations appear in final position, which suggests that, at least, the final vowel did not carry the main accent: Beara ~ Beare, Oco ~ Ocu. In these cases it would seem that Quepo had paroxytone (penult-stressed) words.

5292.dq: Inference from spelling variation of anthroponyms in colonial manuscripts, not from spoken data; no words of the language survive; the statement is explicitly an admission of undeterminability with a speculative paroxytone hint.
5292.prule: Author states accent position (and a fortiori tone) cannot be determined from the surviving material (16th-17th c. Spanish transcriptions of proper names); the only hint is that final-vowel spelling alternations (Beara~Beare, Oco~Ocu) suggest the final vowel was unstressed, i.e. possibly penultimate stress in those names; Areba~Arebe~Aribe, if one name, would be antepenultimate.
5292.quote: Nada, o casi nada, se puede decir del acento -mucho menos del tono- en quepo, ya que, en primer lugar, no existe ninguna palabra en este idioma que haya sobrevivido; en segundo lugar, los materiales con que se cuenta para el presente estudio no permiten identificar posiciones acentuales, debido a la escasez de datos. En algunos casos se presentan alternancias vocálicas en posición final, lo cual da a entender que, al menos, la vocal final no llevaba el acento principal: Beara - Beare, Oco - Ocu. En estos casos, pareciera que el quepo tenía palabras graves.
5292.loc: p. 69, section 3.4 '¿Acento o tono en quepo?'
5292.idn: Quepo, the extinct language of the Quepos of the southern Pacific region of Costa Rica (provincia de Quepo), known only from anthroponyms in 16th-17th century Spanish manuscripts.
5292.exq_: Areba - Arebe - Aribe: if the same anthroponym, 'sería un caso de palabra esdrújula' (antepenult), since only initial <a> is invariant; author flags no certainty it is one name.

5299.quote: 2. Tone. Maꞌdi Urúléti is spoken with tone. There are three main tone levels: high, mid, and low. The tone marks are placed above the vowels. High tone is marked with a line slanting up, low tone is marked with a line slanting down, while mid tone is unmarked. ... A few examples of why using tone marks is important for writing: orí 'snake', òrì 'fear', òrí 'lice'; tí 'cow', ti 'mouth', tì 'to flood'. ... 3. Long vowels ... 5300.quote: Wagarabai is spoken on the Wagarabai River, a tributary of the August River, north-west of Mianmin. The estimated number of speakers is 500 or more. Healey 1964b is the only published source of data on the language. The phonemic system contains the following consonants and vowels: p [p, b], t, k, d, l, m, n, ŋ, f, s, h, w, y; i, e, a, o, u.
